name: twenty-develop-app
description: Use when developing or modifying a Twenty app.
---

# When To Use

Pick this skill when the user wants to change what an existing Twenty app *does* — its data model, UI, logic, or workflows. Representative triggers:

- "add a new object to my Twenty app"
- "create a logic function that runs on record create"
- "add a custom field to the company object"
- "build a front component for the deal page"
- "modify an existing entity / object / field"
- "add a workflow with a manual trigger"
- "add roles and permissions to my app"
- "create a standalone page in my app"

Do not use this skill to scaffold a brand-new app (use `create-app`), to sync/deploy/troubleshoot (use `manage-app`), to prepare marketplace assets (use `publish-app`), or to query workspace records (use `use-twenty-mcp`).

# Boundaries

For background on how Twenty apps work — the SDK packages, remotes, sync lifecycle, and rendering model — read `../twenty-official-references/references/concepts/how-apps-work.md`.

Do not scaffold a new app here. Use `create-app` first when the app does not exist.

# Workflow

First, confirm the setup is sane before changing entities. The current directory should be the root of an existing Twenty app:

```bash
test -f package.json
test -f src/application-config.ts
```

If either file is missing, do not edit blindly. Inspect nearby folders to find the app root, or use `create-app` when the app does not exist.

If setup, dependencies, remotes, authentication, sync, build, deploy, logs, or CI/CD are failing, switch to `manage-app` before continuing with entity work.

For app shape and entity file structure, read `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/app-structure.md`.

## Plan Before Editing

For any change involving more than one entity, state the plan back in 3–6 lines before editing: objects extended, fields added, logic functions and post-install hooks declared, whether the app needs UI. Confirm with the user when there is a real choice.

Skip for single-entity edits, renames, and copy fixes.

## Code Organization

Keep logic functions, post-install hooks, and front components narrow. Extract everything that is not the trigger, inputs, writes, rendering shell, or external call:

- `src/utils/<name>.util.ts` — pure helpers (parsers, mappers, formatters).
- `src/front-components/utils/<name>.util.ts` — front-component runtime helpers that are reusable and testable.
- `src/types/<name>.ts` — external API and internal DTO types (one PascalCase type per file).
- `src/<service>-client/<name>.ts` — wrappers around external SDKs or shared HTTP clients. One folder per service, matching Twenty's `*-client` convention.

Kebab-case filenames. One export per file is mandatory for every helper, type, and client file in `src/` — never multiple function exports in one file. The rule counts exports: a local (non-exported) type may stay alongside the util, but once a type is exported or reused it splits into a `src/types/<name>.ts` file separate from the `src/utils/<name>.util.ts` file. See `app-structure.md` for the canonical rule and the full suffix convention.

Refactor when:

- A `*.logic-function.ts` or `*.post-install.ts` file exceeds the soft cap (see `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/logic.md`).
- A front component contains duplicated command execution, record loading, logic-function lookup, payload building, result parsing, or snackbar formatting.
- The same parsing or mapping logic appears across object types.
- Multiple field files differ only by name and identifier — use a factory under `src/fields/`.

Always create a `*.spec.ts` test file in a sibling `__tests__/` folder for every util/function you add or change, one spec file per source file. See `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/tests.md`.

When a front component triggers a logic function for selected records, always prefer a bulk-capable logic function unless the user explicitly states that the function is only for one record. The default payload shape is `records: Array<{ id: string; ...fields }>`: inside `records`, use `id` for the Twenty record ID because the array name already establishes the record context. Do not add flat single-record compatibility payloads unless the user explicitly asks to preserve an existing single-record API.

## Adding New Entities

Use the app CLI to add new entities. It generates the correct file structure, UUIDs, SDK imports, and boilerplate automatically:

```bash
yarn twenty dev:add
```

This is the default and preferred way to create objects, fields, views, logic functions, front components, and other entities. Do not manually create entity files, explore SDK typings in `node_modules`, or generate UUIDs by hand when the CLI can do it.

Only create entity files manually when modifying existing entities or when the CLI does not support the specific entity type.

## After Entity Changes

Once all edits for the change are complete, run lint and typecheck once at the end (not after each individual edit), then sync the app to the active remote:

```bash
yarn twenty dev:typecheck
yarn lint
yarn twenty apply
```

`yarn twenty dev:typecheck` checks generated app types, `yarn lint` checks local lint rules, and `yarn twenty apply` syncs entity definitions to the active remote. Run all three a single time once every edit is done, not repeatedly after each step. When the user explicitly asks to run tests, follow `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/tests.md`.

Use the official Twenty docs or local SDK source when exact entity fields, imports, or configuration shapes matter.

# Develop References

Read the smallest reference that matches the requested entity work:

- Objects, fields, relations, roles, and permissions: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/data-model.md`
- Views, navigation, page layouts, page layout tabs, and front component registration: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/layout.md`
- Full-page custom UI and standalone page patterns: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/standalone-pages.md`
- Front component source, Twenty UI imports, data hooks, runtime imports, and browser verification: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/front-components.md`
- Logic functions, skills, agents, post-install hooks, and connection providers: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/logic.md`
- Workflows, manual triggers, draft/activate lifecycle, and seeder pitfalls: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/workflows.md`
- Tests — what to cover and where to put the files: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/tests.md`
- App file structure and entity validation checklist: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/app-structure.md`
- Detailed front component UI design: `../../../twenty-official-references/references/design/front-component-ui.md`

For front components, read `front-components.md` before implementation. Use `layout.md` for placement, `standalone-pages.md` for full-page custom UI, and `front-component-ui.md` for visual design and Twenty UI component selection.

# Handoffs

Use `../../../twenty-official-references/references/design/front-component-ui.md` when the entity work turns into front component UI design.

Use `publish-app` when the task turns into README, marketplace copy, screenshots, logos, or listing assets.

  just a title with no spec; when choosing between bare `bv` and `bv --robot-*`;

# beads-north-star — the Jeff-bead standard (durable home)

> **This is the canonical home.** The `beads-br` skill (jsm-managed) carries a mirror
> of this NORTH STAR section that may lag or vanish on the next `jsm install-all
> --force` — it already got wiped once (2026-06-23) and was restored in place as a
> stopgap on 2026-07-01. Do not edit `beads-br`'s SKILL.md to fix drift; fix it here
> and repoint CLAUDE.md's router at this file instead.

Reverse-engineered firsthand from Jeff Emanuel's 11.2k-bead `bv` cockpit (2026-06-17).
**A bead is a SELF-CONTAINED SPEC, not a title.** The full standard + adoption plan:
`~/Developer/foundry/mission/beadflow/JEFF-BEAD-STANDARD-2026-06-17.md`.

## ⛔ `--actor <YourAgentName>` ON EVERY `br` WRITE — NEVER LET IT DEFAULT

**Joshua, 2026-09-07:** *"i dont complete tasks, we shouldn't allow agents to put josh"*

`br` falls back to the **ambient git identity** for `created_by`. A fleet shares one
checkout and therefore one git identity, so every write lands under the human's name.
Measured that day in `uds`:

```
created_by:  156 josh | 48 SapphireIsland | 9 SageCastle | 2 CrimsonCarp | 2 CloudyGrove
assignee:    211 null | 2 SapphireIsland | 2 CloudyGrove | 1 pane3-luna | 1 josh
```

**72% of 217 beads credited the one person who did none of the work.** There is **no
`BEADS_ACTOR` env var** (checked the binary), so the flag is the only lever, and nothing
notices when you omit it.

```bash
br create "..." --actor PinkGorge        # -> created_by=PinkGorge   (proven: uds-508b)
br create "..."                          # -> created_by=josh        (the human, silently)
```

Pass it on **every** write — `create`, `update`, `close`, `comments add`.

**IT IS NOT COSMETIC — IT DEFEATS NON-AUTHOR GRADING.** Grading routes on authorship.
`uds-head-vs-tree-e4qy` read `created_by=josh` while another agent had implemented it;
routing a grader off that field hands an agent **their own bead** and the audit trail
looks *clean* while the closer grades their own work. **So `created_by` is not evidence
of authorship** — when picking a bead to grade, read the bead's comments or ask, never
that field alone.

**Do NOT retro-attribute legacy rows by guess.** Fabricated provenance is worse than
absent provenance (same class as an rch commit stamp that resolves in no repo). Scope any
enforcing detector to a cutoff commit so legacy rows cannot make it vacuously red and get
it disabled.

## CREATE — every non-trivial bead body carries WHAT / WHY / ACCEPTANCE, plus labels

```bash
# -l is MANDATORY (bv navigation) — every `\` below is followed only by a newline (copy-paste-safe;
# a `\` with a trailing inline comment silently breaks the line-continuation).
br create "B6: wire-format conformance harness" \
  --slug wire-format-conformance -t feature -p 1 \
  -l conformance,testing \
  --parent flywheel-<epic> --deps blocks:flywheel-<x> \
  -d 'WHAT: (a) specify wire format; (b) golden/round-trip conformance harness.
WHY: prevents silent drift; public fns currently untested.
ACCEPTANCE: harness green (round-trip+golden+boundary+negative); no public fn/transition lacks a test (AUDITED).'
```

- **WHAT** = the deliverable (enumerate (a)/(b) if multi-part). **WHY** = the pain / what it unblocks.
- **ACCEPTANCE = coverage-shaped, MEASURED, not vibes** — "harness green", "no fn lacks a test", a specific
  closeable condition. This is the close-verify floor (DNA-match to rigor.py / the non-vacuity law).
- **ACCEPTANCE's fires-on-known-bad must be an IN-TREE specimen, never an external apply-patch harness**
  (Jeff's mature-Rust pattern, corpus-grounded 2026-07-06 from frankensqlite / franken_markdown / beads_rust).
  A gate proves it BITES via a `#[test]` that asserts the guard refuses a planted bad input, a trybuild
  compile-fail, or a `--self-test` mode that writes a TEMP fixture and asserts rejection — **never a
  `.patch` + `git apply` + worktree harness.** `git apply` silently no-ops when the patch index-hash misses
  HEAD, so the specimen doesn't fire: a fires-on-known-bad that can't fire is a *fooled certificate = Sev-0*,
  and patches rot against every refactor. Prove-it-bites test: *deleting the guard must turn a test RED*
  (curated `cargo-mutants` on the guard module — not the whole crate — is the tool where a silent hole is Sev-0).
  Prefer **ratchets over thresholds** (a committed monotonic floor / survivor-ceiling that can only improve,
  plus a drift guard tying the number the binary advertises to the number the gate enforces); keep the
  orchestrator (gate.sh / xtask) THIN — assertions live in the tests, not the shell. Full standard + citations:
  the target repo's `docs/RIGOR-STACK.md` (fp's is the reference exemplar).
- **Always `-l <labels>`** (topical, lowercase). **`--slug`** for a readable hierarchical ID. `--parent`/`--deps` for the graph.

## DAG — build backward from the product, then attack closure

A DAG is an execution argument, not a task list. It can be complete only relative to the questions it
planned; never claim absolute completeness.

**Build it:**

1. Start from the buyer-visible terminal outcome and decompose backward. Every leaf must produce an
   input a successor needs, remove a named blocker, or be the terminal product. Presence alone is not
   progress: record the pre-state and require a transition, new call site, or retired incumbent.
2. Add `blocks:` only when the successor cannot satisfy its acceptance without the predecessor's
   output. Put independent checks in cost order: build/import/install before semantic qualification;
   the cheapest falsifier should kill the branch first.
3. Keep the graph reviewable with `bv --robot-plan`, `bv --robot-insights`, and `br graph --all`.
   Before closing the parent, account for every leaf and every blocked terminal; a satisfied
   prerequisite cannot stand in for the closing bead's product.

**Attack each close:**

1. Make acceptance non-vacuous. Demonstrate that the named work changes the pre-state; a condition
   already true before the bead began cannot close it.
2. Make negatives causal. Neutralize unrelated failure preconditions, assert the named detector and
   branch-specific marker, then bypass that detector and prove the same broad RED no longer passes the
   fixture. A nonzero exit alone is not evidence.
3. Bind evidence to the exact source snapshot, executable/artifact identity, and mutable dependency
   identity it tested. Isolate concurrent build outputs. If a bound input moves, revalidate or reopen;
   do not inherit the old green or substitute a fixed age threshold.
4. Assert buyer-visible semantics at the final boundary. For rendered numbers, test the rendered
   label/denominator and audit correct as well as defective sites. For retrieval, token presence is not
   semantic agreement; include a negation control such as `without X`.
5. Reserve one outside-the-plan challenge before epic closure: ask what the real product reads, writes,
   or exposes against its primary buyer data. A planned fixture can catch a defect in what was built;
   it cannot prove the team built the right thing. A new answer becomes a bead, not a retroactive claim
   that the original DAG was complete.
6. Wire each gate to the graph edge controlling the next decision its evidence can invalidate. Ask:
   *what does this stop someone doing tomorrow?* The runtime-backed report/gate in
   `polymarket-pico-z@125d23f2fa96e46d0076e9785979fcf8d7123eba:PLAN-EDGE-MEASUREMENT.md:49-86` had
   zero resolved trades and said no more code before 500, yet the gate at
   `polymarket-pico-z@0944915eebca91cced6496e32d8b1ea1de22cc6d:src/engine/sports_go_live_gate.py:75-147`
   blocked real-money launch, not construction, and was archived on 2026-04-08. Evidence still did
   not establish edge on 2026-04-11, while R16/R18 were CLEAN with zero criticals or mediums
   (`polymarket-pico-z@125d23f2fa96e46d0076e9785979fcf8d7123eba:PLAN-REVIEWS/round18-adversarial.md:96-114`).
   Contrast `bughunt-platform-plan@1933524b05123ffc1d7985a106a22d2ada5a73f3:.flywheel/CHARTER.md:7-47`,
   whose premise review halted construction. A terminal-only gate is a gate on nothing while distant.

**Measured sources** (all in `~/Developer/franken-harvest`): bead `fh-xjj` (presence passed while
adoption stayed zero), `standards/causal-known-bads.md` and bead `fh-kkf` (11/24 to 24/24 causal),
`standards/hermetic-shared-tree-tests.md` and bead `fh-t36` (stale binary passed 2/2), bead `fh-ost`
(53 upstream moves/30d; median 12.49h), bead `fh-vyl` (cheap filter removed 3/5 before qualification),
and bead `fh-1v5` (luv-diet rendered, negation, and unplanned-question evidence).

**Rejected, deliberately:** a universal 12.49-hour expiry (C20 supplied a measured cadence, not a
portable clock); C33/C34's literal food/UI wording as separate DAG rules (their boundary patterns are
retained above); and a mandatory DAG-proof document or meta-bead (it would manufacture an artifact
solely for checking). No other measured candidate was discarded.

## REVIEW / READ / PLAN — `bv` is the planning BRAIN, not just a list

Jeff's cockpit; we underuse it:

```bash
# the navigation half — how Jeff reads/plans an 11k beadbase (all --robot-* = JSON for agents):
bv --robot-triage                 # unified ranked work + evidence (THE default; what to do)
bv --robot-next                   # the single best next bead
bv --robot-plan                   # dependency-respecting execution ORDER
bv --robot-priority               # priority recommendations
bv --robot-insights               # graph analysis: centrality, impact, structure (the per-bead metrics)
bv --robot-triage-by-track        # group by execution track (multi-agent coordination)
bv -r actionable | high-impact    # named recipes
bv -l <label> --robot-insights    # SCOPE analysis to one label's subgraph (needs labels — see Step 3)
bv --severity warning --alert-type stale_issue   # the ALERTS surface (Jeff's "⚠ N alerts")
br scheduler --json               # explainable ranked dispatch for swarms (PageRank + staleness + fairness)
br show <id> --json   ·   br ready --json   ·   br blocked --json   ·   br graph --all
```

A HUMAN watches the fleet with bare `bv` (the full-screen TUI cockpit — his screen). An AGENT never runs
bare `bv` (blocks in TUI) — always `bv --robot-*`. **`-l <label>` scoping + the alert surface only work if
beads are labeled** — our labels are at 32% with 1,199-label sprawl; consolidation is the Step-3 enabler.

## HANDLE — the audit trail lives IN the bead

Our biggest gap: only 8% have comments; Jeff's are the norm.

```bash
br comments add flywheel-<id> "COVERAGE AUDIT (read-only): 82/84 paths covered; round-trip+golden green. \
VERDICT: satisfied; 2 gaps low-risk. @<agent> hold 2 tests."   # at every close/checkpoint
br close flywheel-<id> --reason "<what+proof>"                   # reason carries WHAT + the proof/receipt
```

At every close or checkpoint, add a comment with a **VERDICT** — don't bury the verification in commits/chat.

**The verb is `br comments` (PLURAL). `br comment` never posts — and its failure exits 0.**
`comment` is clap **prefix-matching** to `comments`, so your text lands where a *subcommand* was
expected. Both forms below pass a body correctly; `--file` is for long or quote-heavy text, not a
requirement:

```bash
br comments add <id> "VERDICT: …"          # correct — positional string persists
br comments add <id> --file <path>         # correct — same thing, for long/quote-heavy bodies
br comment     <id> "VERDICT: …"           # NEVER

# Using MCP Agent Mail

> **Core Insight:** Without coordination, multiple agents overwrite each other's work. Agent Mail provides identities, messaging, and file reservations to prevent conflicts.

## When to Use What

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Starting any agent session | `macro_start_session` |
| About to edit files | `file_reservation_paths` → edit → `release_file_reservations` |
| Need to tell another agent something | `send_message` with `thread_id` |
| Picking up someone else's work | `macro_prepare_thread` |
| Can't message an agent | `request_contact` → wait for approval |
| Server seems broken | Use `health_check()` first; CLI-only: `doctor check --verbose` → `doctor repair --yes` |

---

## THE EXACT PROMPT — Session Bootstrap

**Call this at the start of every agent session:**

```
macro_start_session(
  human_key="/abs/path/to/project",
  program="claude-code",
  model="YOUR_MODEL",
  task_description="Working on auth module"
)
```

Returns: `{project, agent, file_reservations, inbox}`

This single call: ensures project exists → registers your identity → fetches inbox.

---

## Core Operations

| Task | Tool |
|------|------|
| Bootstrap session | `macro_start_session(human_key, program, model, task_description)` |
| Send message | `send_message(project_key, sender_name, to, subject, body_md)` |
| Reply in thread | `reply_message(project_key, message_id, sender_name, body_md)` |
| Check inbox | `fetch_inbox(project_key, agent_name, limit=20)` |
| Reserve files | `file_reservation_paths(project_key, agent_name, paths, ttl_seconds)` |
| Release files | `release_file_reservations(project_key, agent_name)` |
| Search messages | `search_messages(project_key, "query")` |

### The Four Macros

| Macro | When to Use |
|-------|-------------|
| `macro_start_session` | Bootstrap: project → agent → inbox |
| `macro_prepare_thread` | Join existing thread with summary |
| `macro_file_reservation_cycle` | Reserve → work → auto-release |
| `macro_contact_handshake` | Cross-agent contact setup |

### Fast Resource Reads (No Tool Call Required)

| Need | Resource |
|------|----------|
| List agents | `resource://agents/{project_key}` |
| Inbox | `resource://inbox/{agent}?project=/abs/path&limit=20` |
| Thread | `resource://thread/{thread_id}?project=/abs/path&include_bodies=true` |
| Ack-required | `resource://views/ack-required/{agent}?project=/abs/path` |

---

## File Reservations

### Reserve Before Editing

```
file_reservation_paths(
  project_key="/abs/path/project",
  agent_name="GreenCastle",
  paths=["src/auth/**/*.ts"],
  ttl_seconds=3600,
  exclusive=true,
  reason="bd-123"
)
```

Returns: `{granted: [...], conflicts: [...]}`

### Conflict Resolution

If conflicts exist:
1. **Wait** — TTL will expire
2. **Coordinate** — Message the holder
3. **Share** — Use `exclusive=false`

### Release When Done

```
release_file_reservations(project_key="/abs/path/project", agent_name="GreenCastle")
```

---

## Beads Integration

Use bead IDs as your threading anchor:

```
1. Pick work:        br ready --json → choose bd-123
2. Reserve files:    file_reservation_paths(..., reason="bd-123")
3. Announce:         send_message(..., thread_id="bd-123", subject="[bd-123] Starting...")
4. Work:             Reply in thread with progress
5. Complete:         br close bd-123, release_file_reservations(...), final message
```

**Bead ID (often bd-###) goes in:** thread_id, subject prefix, reservation reason, commit message

---

## Quick Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| "sender_name not registered" | Call `macro_start_session` first |
| "FILE_RESERVATION_CONFLICT" | Wait, coordinate, or use `exclusive=false` |
| "CONTACT_BLOCKED" | Use `request_contact`, wait for approval |
| Empty inbox | Check `since_ts`, `urgent_only`, agent name spelling |
| Server unreachable | Use `health_check()` or `resource://config/environment` to confirm MCP server is up; if CLI-only, check `curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/health` |
| Guard blocks commit | Set `AGENT_NAME` env var; bypass: `AGENT_MAIL_BYPASS=1 git commit` |

```bash
# Quick health check (CLI daemon)
curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/health

# Full diagnostics (CLI)
uv run python -m mcp_agent_mail.cli doctor check --verbose

# Preview repairs (dry run, CLI)
uv run python -m mcp_agent_mail.cli doctor repair --dry-run

# Apply repairs (CLI)
uv run python -m mcp_agent_mail.cli doctor repair --yes
```

register_agent(

# beads-bv — Graph-Aware Triage

<!-- TOC: Robot Mode | Commands | Workflow | Scoping | Metrics | br | Troubleshooting | References -->

> **Core Insight:** Your backlog is a directed graph. PageRank finds what everything depends on. Betweenness finds bottlenecks. The math knows your priorities better than your gut.

## CRITICAL: Robot Mode Only

```bash
bv                    # WRONG — launches TUI, blocks terminal
bv --robot-triage     # CORRECT — JSON output for agents
```

**NEVER run bare `bv` in agent contexts.**

---

## Commands

### Core (Start Here)

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-triage` | THE MEGA-COMMAND: recommendations + blockers + health | What should I work on? |
| `--robot-next` | Single top pick + claim command | Just the one thing |
| `--robot-plan` | Parallel execution tracks with `unblocks` | What can run concurrently? |
| `--robot-insights` | All metrics + cycles + density + k-core + slack | Deep analysis |
| `--robot-priority` | Priority misalignments with confidence | Am I prioritizing wrong? |

### Labels & Health

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-label-health` | Per-label: health_level, velocity, staleness | Which domain is struggling? |
| `--robot-label-flow` | Cross-label dependencies, bottleneck_labels | Inter-team blockers |
| `--robot-label-attention` | Attention-ranked labels | Where to focus? |
| `--robot-alerts` | Stale issues, blocking cascades, priority mismatches | What's rotting? |
| `--robot-suggest` | Duplicates, missing deps, cycle breaks | Hygiene |

### History & Correlation

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-history` | Bead-to-commit correlations | Change tracking |
| `--robot-causality <id>` | Timeline, blockers, insights | Why did this take so long? |
| `--robot-related <id>` | File/commit overlap, clusters | What's connected? |
| `--robot-file-beads <path>` | Beads that touched a file | Code ownership |

### Time-Travel & Search

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-diff --diff-since <ref>` | New/closed/modified since ref | What changed? |
| `--as-of <ref>` | Historical point-in-time | Time-travel |
| `--robot-search` | Search results as JSON | Find beads |
| `--search-mode hybrid` | Text + graph ranking | Smart search |

**Full command reference:** [COMMANDS.md](references/COMMANDS.md)

---

## Workflow

```bash
# 1. What should I work on?
bv --robot-triage | jq '.triage.recommendations[0]'

# 2. Claim it
br update bd-123 --status in_progress

# 3. Do the work...

# 4. Done
br close bd-123 --reason "Implemented in abc123"

# 5. Next
bv --robot-triage
```

---

## Scoping & Filtering

```bash
bv --robot-plan --label backend              # Scope to label's subgraph
bv --robot-insights --as-of HEAD~30          # Historical point-in-time
bv --recipe actionable --robot-plan          # Only unblocked items
bv --recipe high-impact --robot-triage       # Top PageRank scores
bv --robot-triage --robot-triage-by-track    # Group by parallel streams
bv --robot-triage --robot-triage-by-label    # Group by domain
bv --robot-alerts --severity=critical        # Filter alerts
```

---

## Key Metrics

| Metric | High Score Means |
|--------|------------------|
| **PageRank** | Everything depends on this — fix first |
| **Betweenness** | Bottleneck — blocks multiple paths |
| **Cycles** | **Broken graph — fix immediately** |
| **K-Core** | Structural strength (core membership) |
| **Articulation** | Cut vertex — removal disconnects graph |

### Decision Matrix

| Pattern | Meaning | Action |
|---------|---------|--------|
| High PageRank + High Betweenness | Critical bottleneck | Drop everything, fix this |
| High PageRank + Low Betweenness | Foundation piece | Important but not blocking |
| Low PageRank + High Betweenness | Unexpected chokepoint | Investigate why |

**Full metrics:** [METRICS.md](references/METRICS.md)

---

## br Essentials

```bash
br ready --json                              # What's unblocked?
br create "Title" -d "desc"                  # New issue
br update bd-123 --status in_progress        # Working on this
br close bd-123 --reason "Done"              # Done
br dep add bd-123 bd-456                      # Add dependency
br dep remove bd-123 bd-456                   # Break cycle
```

---

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `bv` hangs | TUI launched | Use `--robot-*` flags |
| Cycles detected | Circular dependency | `br dep remove` to break |
| Phase 2 timeout | Large graph (>500 nodes) | Check `status` field |
| Empty metric maps | Phase 2 still running | Check `status` flags |
| Inconsistent outputs | Different data | Compare `data_hash` |

---

```bash
# Tools working?
bv --robot-triage >/dev/null && br list >/dev/null && echo "OK"

# Graph healthy?
bv --robot-insights | jq '{cycles: .Cycles, density: .ClusterDensity}'
# cycles must be [], density < 0.3 is healthy
```

1:# UDS gate contract
2:
3:## Purpose
4:
5:UDS has one ordered verdict chain. It answers whether the repository is measurable and what stopped
6:measurement; it does not convert a refusal, timeout, or missing input into a product PASS.
7:## Gate wiring
8:
9:The tracked scripts/check.sh dispatcher is the canonical ordered consumer of this contract. The repository pre-commit wrapper is githooks/pre-commit; the commit-message wrapper is githooks/commit-msg; both delegate to tracked executable implementations. Each gate must preserve the typed exit lattice and carry a fires-on-known-bad leg.
10:
11:The pre-commit implementation checks staged whitespace with `git diff --cached --check`, then invokes the existing autofix tool with `--check --staged --repo`. Check mode does not rewrite worktree files or restage partial edits. The external helper selects staged path names but currently reads their worktree bytes; general staged-blob formatter isolation is not established. Staged-deletion and Beads JSONL guards remain required.
12:
13:## Gate sentence
14:
15:The chain is the existing `scripts/check.sh` stage sequence. `closure` is last because it joins the
16:registry, planning spine, bead graph, and scorecard. A failed earlier stage blocks later stages;
17:blocked is not a verdict for the blocked subject.
18:
19:```text
20:fmt -> clippy -> test -> registry-check -> neg-evidence-gate -> close-evidence-gate
21:    -> dag-validate-gate -> build-intent -> claims-lint -> conformance -> build-placement
22:    -> artifact-platform -> close-cites -> bead-commit-check -> scorecard-promotion
23:    -> review-lineage-check -> closure
24:```
25:
26:Seventeen stages, copied from the `STAGES=(...)` array at `scripts/check.sh:16` rather than
27:restated from memory. The `G1`-`G11` contracts below name **eleven** of them. The other six are
28:`neg-evidence-gate`, `close-evidence-gate` and `dag-validate-gate` (documented under *House gate
29:wiring*), plus `artifact-platform`, `bead-commit-check` and `review-lineage-check`, which have **no
30:gate contract in this document**. That gap is stated rather than hidden: a chain longer than its
31:contract is how a stage runs with nobody able to say what it reads.
32:
33:## Typed result law
34:
35:The typed exit lattice is defined by `crates/uds/src/lib.rs`:
36:
37:| code | meaning | law |
38:|---|---|---|
39:| `EC-PASS` | the operation ran and succeeded | only a completed positive verdict |
40:| `EC-RED` | a named guard or genuine gated defect fired | subject failure, not a count |
41:| `EC-USAGE` | the invocation was invalid | repair the caller |
42:| `EC-LOCKED` | another writer/build holds the lease | `EL-LOCK-IS-NOT-FAILURE` |
43:| `EC-UNRUN` | the subject could not be measured | `EL-UNRUN-IS-NOT-RED` |
44:| `EC-INFRA` | the gate's own machinery failed | `EL-INFRA-IS-NOT-SUBJECT` |
45:| `EC-TIMEOUT` | a bounded stage was killed by its wall clock | timeout is not a subject verdict |
46:
47:The three laws are source-defined at `crates/uds/src/lib.rs`: `EL-LOCK-IS-NOT-FAILURE`,
48:`EL-UNRUN-IS-NOT-RED`, and `EL-INFRA-IS-NOT-SUBJECT`. A gate must preserve their distinctions.
49:
50:## Gate contracts
51:
52:### G1 — format
53:
54:Command: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, invoked by `scripts/check.sh`.
55:
56:Subject: the tree at `HEAD`, not the worktree — the stage row prints `fmt_subject=HEAD`, and
57:`run_fmt_head` (`scripts/check.sh:136`) formats a `mktemp -d` snapshot of `HEAD`. Uncommitted
58:formatting therefore does not clear this gate, and committed unformatted code REDs it for everyone.
59:
60:Known negative evidence: `scripts/check.sh --selftest` plants a failing command for this stage in a
61:`mktemp` file under `$TMPDIR` and asserts the failure is named and every later stage prints
62:`BLOCKED <stage> after=fmt`. That is evidence the dispatch chain recognizes a format failure, not
63:evidence the current source is formatted. The current verdict must be read from a fresh chain
64:run.
65:
66:### G2 — clippy
67:
68:Command: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, routed through the existing
69:remote build path in `scripts/check.sh`.
70:
71:Known negative evidence: the `--selftest` planted leg for this stage, named and downstream-blocked
72:as above. No green claim is made from a planted leg.
73:
74:Known defect: this stage cannot currently execute at all. Its command contains a bare `--`, which
75:`scripts/worker-input-drift.py` refuses (`uds-oiw9`), and the refusal is rendered as `RED clippy`
76:(`uds-jqb1`). See *Current verdict*.
77:
78:### G3 — tests
79:
80:Command: `cargo test -j 2 --workspace`, routed through the existing remote build path.
81:
82:Known negative evidence: the `--selftest` planted leg for this stage, named and downstream-blocked
83:as above. A test process that cannot run is `EC-UNRUN`; a failed test is `EC-RED`.
84:
85:### G4 — registry checks
86:
87:Command: `cargo run -q -p registry-check -- all`, routed through the existing remote build path.
88:The registry check must reject empty or malformed registry inputs by a named detector. The stage
89:refuses an empty scan set before running (`scripts/check.sh:228-233`, exit 77). Its planted leg is
90:the `--selftest` one described above. No registry subject is claimed green here.
91:
92:Known defect: like G2, this stage's command carries a bare `--` and is currently unreachable
93:(`uds-oiw9`).
94:
95:### G5 — build intent
96:
97:Command: `cargo run -q -p registry-check -- build-intent`, routed through the existing remote
98:build path. The subject derives toolchain, lockfile, git-source, and source-replacement inputs;
99:empty input is `EC-UNRUN`, abbreviated/floating/mismatched input is a named RED finding.
100:
101:### G6 — claims lint
102:
103:Command: `cargo run -q -p registry-check -- claims-lint`, routed through the existing remote build
104:path. It checks the declared claims registry and named scan roots; an absent declared root is not a
105:silent pass.
106:
107:### G7 — conformance
108:
109:Command: `cargo test -p uds-drift --test differential --locked`, routed through the existing remote
110:build path. The differential oracle is external to the subject implementation; an unavailable
111:oracle is UNRUN, not a passing comparison.
112:
113:### G8 — build placement
114:
115:Command: `scripts/cargo-route-gate.py`, invoked by the existing chain. Every cargo compilation must
116:carry the remote route; an empty scan is UNRUN and a local-only cargo path is RED.
117:
118:### G9 — close-cites
119:
120:Command: `cargo run -q -p close-cites --locked -- --repo-root <root>`. It checks closed-bead
121:selftest citations against tracked evidence while distinguishing destroyed mutation fixtures from
122:surviving evidence. Empty closed-with-citation input is UNRUN.
123:
124:### G10 — scorecard promotion
125:
126:Command: `python3 docs/contracts/scorecard_promotion_check.py --repo-root <root>`. It derives every
127:scorecard row and evidence path, executes named predicates under their bounded contract, and keeps
128:missing, prose, directory, non-PASS, and predicate-failed states visible. It does not write a
129:scorecard row.
130:
131:### G11 — closure
132:
133:Command: `cargo run -q -p closure-check --locked -- --repo-root <root> --structural`. It joins the
134:registry, plan graph, bead graph, and scorecard. A structural result is not a publish or public-flip
135:authorization.
136:
137:## The G1-G8 ladder
138:This is the executable ladder inventory. Each row names the external oracle, the fail-closed rule,
139:the planted defect that must turn it RED, and the reachable trigger that runs it. UNQUANTIFIED(G2)
140:and UNQUANTIFIED(G5) are deliberate qualitative exceptions; G9-G11 are downstream qualitative
141:gates outside this quantified set.
142:
143:| gate | external oracle | quantified fail-closed rule | fires-on-known-bad | reachable trigger |
144:|---|---|---|---|---|
145:| G1 | rustfmt toolchain; its formatter result is independent of UDS semantics | TH-GATE-G1-FORMAT, violations <= 0 | introduce a rustfmt diff; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo fmt --all -- --check must fail | scripts/check.sh stage fmt |
146:| G2 | workspace tests and refusal tests; qualitative consistency oracle | UNQUANTIFIED(G2) — no numeric floor by design | plant the --selftest leg for the test stage; scripts/check.sh --selftest must name the failure and block downstream | scripts/check.sh stage test |
147:| G3 | frozen conformance/oracles/ twin via differential comparison | TH-GATE-G3-DIFFERENTIAL, mismatches <= 0 | introduce a differential mismatch in the conformance fixture; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo test -p uds-drift --test differential --locked must fail | scripts/check.sh stage conformance |
148:| G4 | caller-path artifact resolved by command -v, file, and uds version | TH-GATE-G4-VERSION, version_proofs >= 1 | place a shadow uds earlier on PATH or make its version unparseable; uds doctor must refuse caller identity | uds doctor |
149:| G5 | planted-negative dispatcher under test | UNQUANTIFIED(G5) — qualitative reachability rule by design | plant the --selftest leg for a dispatched stage; bash scripts/check.sh --selftest must name the failure and block downstream | scripts/check.sh --selftest |
150:| G6 | seeded fuzz corpus, not a self-reported coverage claim | TH-GATE-G6-FUZZ, seeded_cases >= 1 | remove every seed from fuzz/corpus; registry-check fuzz-wiring must refuse the empty corpus | scripts/check.sh registry-check stage |
151:| G7 | component proof receipts and per-component evidence paths | TH-GATE-G7-COMPONENT, unrun_rows <= 0 | mark one required component receipt UNRUN; scripts/check.sh stage scorecard-promotion must block it | scripts/check.sh stage scorecard-promotion |
152:| G8 | publishability scorecard evaluated by the promotion predicate | TH-GATE-G8-PUBLISH, open_rows <= 0 | add an OPEN scorecard row; python3 docs/contracts/scorecard_promotion_check.py --repo-root . must refuse promotion | scripts/check.sh stage scorecard-promotion |
153:
154:G2/G5 are explicitly qualitative and G9/G10/G11 remain downstream; no threshold row is invented
155:for them. Every quantified identifier above must exist in registries/thresholds.toml.
156:
157:## Oracle
158:The ladder has two layers. G1-G8 are the oracle ladder; G9-G11 are downstream evidence/closure
159:gates. The oracle is named separately from the subject: a passing command does not prove a different
160:boundary than the one it reads.
161:
162:| gate | oracle and runnable command | does not prove |
163:|---|---|---|
164:| G1 | rustfmt; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo fmt --all -- --check | no semantic correctness or installed-artifact identity |
165:| G2 | workspace tests/refusals; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo test --locked -j 2 --workspace | no external behavioral oracle; qualitative and unquantified by design |
166:| G3 | frozen conformance/oracles twin; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo test -p uds-drift --test differential --locked | no proof that the installed caller is this source |
167:| G4 | caller-path artifact; BIN=$(command -v uds); file -b "$BIN"; "$BIN" version | no conformance claim about behavior |
168:| G5 | planted-negative dispatcher; bash scripts/check.sh --selftest | no product defect coverage beyond reachable selftest legs; qualitative and unquantified by design |
169:| G6 | seeded corpus; find fuzz/corpus -type f -print -quit | no fuzz correctness or coverage claim |
170:| G7 | component proof receipts; bash scripts/check.sh and component-proof evidence paths | no claim that an UNRUN component is proven |
171:| G8 | publishability scorecard; python3 docs/contracts/scorecard_promotion_check.py --repo-root . | no authorization to make the public flip |
172:| G9 | close-cites; RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo run --locked -p close-cites -- --repo-root . | no product PASS from a citation alone |
173:| G10 | scorecard promotion; pytho

name: agent-mail
description: >-
  MCP Agent Mail for multi-agent coordination. Use when agents need file locks,
  messaging, inboxes, or conflict prevention. Handles macro_start_session,
  file_reservation_paths, send_message, threading, pre-commit guards.
---

<!-- TOC: Bootstrap | Core Ops | File Reservations | Beads | Troubleshooting | Identity | Human Overseer | Pre-Commit Guard | References -->

# Using MCP Agent Mail

> **Core Insight:** Without coordination, multiple agents overwrite each other's work. Agent Mail provides identities, messaging, and file reservations to prevent conflicts.

## When to Use What

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Starting any agent session | `macro_start_session` |
| About to edit files | `file_reservation_paths` → edit → `release_file_reservations` |
| Need to tell another agent something | `send_message` with `thread_id` |
| Picking up someone else's work | `macro_prepare_thread` |
| Can't message an agent | `request_contact` → wait for approval |
| Server seems broken | Use `health_check()` first; CLI-only: `am doctor check --verbose` → `am doctor repair --dry-run` → `am doctor repair --yes` |

---

## THE EXACT PROMPT — Session Bootstrap

**Call this at the start of every agent session:**

```
macro_start_session(
  human_key="/abs/path/to/project",
  program="claude-code",
  model="YOUR_MODEL",
  task_description="Working on auth module"
)
```

Returns: `{project, agent, file_reservations, inbox}`

This single call: ensures project exists → registers your identity → fetches inbox.

---

## Core Operations

| Task | Tool |
|------|------|
| Bootstrap session | `macro_start_session(human_key, program, model, task_description)` |
| Send message | `send_message(project_key, sender_name, to, subject, body_md)` |
| Reply in thread | `reply_message(project_key, message_id, sender_name, body_md)` |
| Check inbox | `fetch_inbox(project_key, agent_name, limit=20)` |
| Reserve files | `file_reservation_paths(project_key, agent_name, paths, ttl_seconds)` |
| Release files | `release_file_reservations(project_key, agent_name)` |
| Search messages | `search_messages(project_key, "query")` |

### The Four Macros

| Macro | When to Use |
|-------|-------------|
| `macro_start_session` | Bootstrap: project → agent → inbox |
| `macro_prepare_thread` | Join existing thread with summary |
| `macro_file_reservation_cycle` | Reserve in one call; `auto_release=true` releases before it returns |
| `macro_contact_handshake` | Cross-agent contact setup |

### Fast Resource Reads (No Tool Call Required)

| Need | Resource |
|------|----------|
| List agents | `resource://agents/{project_key}` |
| Inbox | `resource://inbox/{agent}?project=/abs/path&limit=20` |
| Thread | `resource://thread/{thread_id}?project=/abs/path&include_bodies=true` |
| Ack-required | `resource://views/ack-required/{agent}?project=/abs/path` |

---

## File Reservations

### Reserve Before Editing

```
file_reservation_paths(
  project_key="/abs/path/project",
  agent_name="GreenCastle",
  paths=["src/auth/**/*.ts"],
  ttl_seconds=3600,
  exclusive=true,
  reason="bd-123"
)
```

Returns: `{granted: [...], conflicts: [...]}`. Conflicting paths are left out of `granted`.

### Conflict Resolution

If conflicts exist:
1. **Wait** — TTL will expire
2. **Coordinate** — Message the holder
3. **Share** — Use `exclusive=false` (only helps when the holder's reservation is also shared; a shared request still conflicts with an exclusive one)

### Release When Done

```
release_file_reservations(project_key="/abs/path/project", agent_name="GreenCastle")
```

---

## Beads Integration

Use bead IDs as your threading anchor:

```
1. Pick work:        br ready --json → choose bd-123
2. Reserve files:    file_reservation_paths(..., reason="bd-123")
3. Announce:         send_message(..., thread_id="bd-123", subject="[bd-123] Starting...")
4. Work:             Reply in thread with progress
5. Complete:         br close bd-123, release_file_reservations(...), final message
```

**Bead ID (often bd-###) goes in:** thread_id, subject prefix, reservation reason, commit message

---

## Quick Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| `NOT_FOUND`: "Agent 'X' not found in project" | Call `macro_start_session` first, or check the name via `resource://agents/{project_key}` |
| Non-empty `conflicts` in a reservation result | Wait, coordinate, or (if the holder is shared) use `exclusive=false` |
| "CONTACT_BLOCKED" | Use `request_contact`, wait for approval |
| Empty inbox | Check `since_ts`, `urgent_only`, agent name spelling |
| Server unreachable | Use `health_check()` or `resource://config/environment` to confirm MCP server is up; if CLI-only, check `curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/health` |
| Guard blocks commit | Set `AGENT_NAME` env var; bypass: `AGENT_MAIL_BYPASS=1 git commit` |

### Doctor Diagnostics (CLI-only, optional)

```bash
# Quick health check (CLI daemon)
curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/health

# Full diagnostics (CLI)
am doctor check --verbose

# Preview repairs (dry run, CLI)
am doctor repair --dry-run

# Apply repairs (CLI; refuses with exit 3 while a live mailbox owner holds the DB)
am doctor repair --yes
```

---

## Agent Identity

Agents get adjective+noun names: GreenCastle, BlueLake, RedBear.

**Best practice:** Omit `name` parameter to auto-generate valid names.

```
register_agent(
  project_key="/abs/path/project",
  program="claude-code",
  model="YOUR_MODEL",
  task_description="Auth refactor"
)  # name auto-generated
```

---

## Human Overseer

Send priority messages to agents from the web UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/mail`:

1. Open the project page, then its overseer compose link (`/mail/{project_slug}/overseer/compose`)
2. Select explicit target agents (broadcast is not supported)
3. Send; overseer messages are always sent with `importance: high` and a "MESSAGE FROM HUMAN OVERSEER" preamble

Agents see them via `fetch_inbox(..., urgent_only=true)` (which matches high and urgent).

---

## Pre-Commit Guard

```
install_precommit_guard(project_key="/abs/path", code_repo_path="/abs/path")
```

- Set `AGENT_NAME` env var so guard knows who you are
- Bypass emergency: `AGENT_MAIL_BYPASS=1 git commit -m "fix"`
- Warning mode: `AGENT_MAIL_GUARD_MODE=warn`

---

## Search Syntax (Search V3)

```
"exact phrase"
prefix*
term1 AND term2
term1 OR term2
auth AND NOT admin
```

Parentheses are stripped before parsing, so they do not group terms.

# Twenty ecosystem mission plan — app-factory lane (P01–P18)

> **Section owner:** cfsios pane 4, MaroonForge. This is a proposed implementation plan, not an execution receipt.
> **Status:** drafted 2026-09-30; no implementation, install, Railway operation, release, production access, or acceptance test was performed by this author.
> **Integration:** the mission-plan owner merges this section into the parent plan, resolves cross-lane edges, and owns final plan review and Beads conversion.
> **Path status:** every `PROPOSED` repository, file, command, service, URL, and test target below is a planned artifact, not a claim that it exists.

## Mission outcome

Build a portable, installable Twenty app factory that gives ClutterFreeSpaces a useful operating surface and gives other operators a safe way to author, review, validate, install, and update independently versioned Twenty apps.

Joshua/CFS is the first user and the first demanding acceptance environment; the starter is free under MIT. The public developer CLI and reusable app library are distinct public repositories. Private CFS workflows, records, credentials, client documents, subscription-only skills, and internal prompts remain outside both repositories.

This lane is not a ninth-app cap. Growth Lead Desk is the first proving phase across every lead channel actually verified in the CFS evidence. It is not evidence that later phases must be selected from a fixed list. The separate recovery worker's search for later candidates remains an input to the parent mission; this section does not invent or pre-select those candidates.

The factory must ship buyer-usable capability, not only manifests, docs, CI, scorecards, or install success. Product-delivery cards keep their implementation, permanent behavior tests, mounted consumer, and observable runtime proof together. P01 is the explicit no-code planning/bootstrap exception: it initializes local library governance and its Beads DAG, earns no product-delivery credit, and does not require a first app or mounted consumer.

## Settled decisions and boundaries

|Area|Decision for this plan|Boundary / proof obligation|
|---|---|---|
|First user and price|Joshua/CFS first; free MIT starting point.|MIT applies to first-party public code only after third-party notices and source provenance are cleared.|
|Public developer CLI|Dedicated public TypeScript CLI repo, working name `twy`, proposed root `/Users/josh/Developer/twy`.|F01 owns CLI-repository bootstrap/governance; its own `AGENTS.md`, package/release lifecycle, and Beads DAG; never import CFS client data or runtime secrets.|
|Public app library|Separate public repo, proposed root `/Users/josh/Developer/twenty-apps`.|Downloadable apps are native Twenty server-app packages with declared, verified external dependencies; they do not bundle a Node server/runtime. The CLI is separate software with its own Node runtime/package.|
|CFS adapter|Private/local adapters and CFS-only app code stay in this repository.|The public package consumes an explicit interface; it must not import private records, private docs, credentials, or retired-console code.|
|Twenty integration|Official supported Twenty app SDK/API and external adapters; no server fork.|Pin and prove the installed core contract. A newer SDK manual is not proof of 2.41 runtime compatibility.|
|Operator UI|Prefer native Twenty surfaces for authenticated staff workflows.|External Cloudflare UI is only for a justified browser boundary such as scoped client self-service; it does not replace the CRM operator surface.|
|Client access|Email sign-in links only after an already-authorized client explicitly requests authentication.|Require a pre-existing client/job grant; no Twenty membership, admin/app-install role, or broad record lookup by email alone.|
|Auth and business email|Send an auth-only sign-in link only when an already-authorized client explicitly requests authentication; all outreach, proposals, invoices, reminders, and other business messages remain manually reviewed.|No login email may piggyback a business message. No sends or activation occur in this planning work; provider/config behavior must be measured, not assumed.|
|Demo/test|Separate team-administered Railway ZestStream synthetic environment.|Separate identity, data, secrets, and service from CFS production and from any public demo; only curated synthetic demo data may be public.|
|Public app ecosystem|Reviewed first-party and third-party apps may enter the library.|Provenance, license, support owner, permission scope, compatibility, install effect, and update/uninstall behavior are visible before install.|
|Version baseline|Twenty 2.41.0 is the first compatibility target.|Re-measure the target at implementation time; 2.43 docs or SDK examples do not satisfy a 2.41 proof.|

The working names `twy`, `twenty-apps`, app IDs, aliases, commands, paths, environments, and interfaces in this section are planning identifiers. Names may be changed by the parent plan before Beads creation; changes must preserve the boundaries and acceptance evidence, not fabricate implemented surfaces.

## Architecture contract

1. `twy` is a user-facing developer/administrator CLI for discovering, creating, inspecting, validating, planning, installing, updating, and removing app packages. It is not a second Twenty server, and its own output must never report an app as installed when the target has not been read back.
2. `twenty-apps` is a reviewed source and distribution repository. Each app has a stable Universal Identifier, semver, explicit Twenty engine range, declared permissions and data effects, install instructions, support ownership, and a clean package boundary.
3. A `twy` command may orchestrate the native Twenty CLI/API, but native Twenty remains the mutation mechanism. `yarn twenty app:install` accepts a local `appPath` or the explicit `--remote <name>` flag; it does not accept an arbitrary `remoteAppRef` or `package@version` as equivalent input. Never invent a parallel install protocol or confuse package publication with workspace installation.
4. Metadata apply, app deployment, registry publication, server installation, external UI deployment, Git CI, and release publication are different transitions. Report and verify each independently.
5. `config = null`, query error, unsupported capability, expired credentials, or absent integration is `UNKNOWN`/blocked with a recovery instruction; never infer a usable value or use OAuth client discovery as a fallback.
6. SDK-generated types are compile-time input, not server truth. Inspect relevant source and actual target introspection/payloads; use a version-specific adapter for observed response shape. Do not assume nested SDK objects expose `.fields`; do not claim complete data until root-field and response pagination are exhausted.
7. After isolated semantic checks establish the behavior, the metadata API can read back the exact app Universal Identifier and installed version. That proves identity/version only, not object ownership, fields, views, role scope, navigation, or user-visible behavior; read each back and open the mounted surface.
8. App-scoped client generation is unsupported on the 2.41 baseline. Use an explicit server-side adapter boundary and actor model; do not describe unsupported app-scoped tokens as a secure alternative.
9. `cfsJob` and `cfsPayment` are Custom-owned. `Person` and `Opportunity` are Twenty standard objects. Never redefine Custom-owned entities; do not assume an app can extend a foreign standard-owned field because the CLI exited zero.
10. Every shared row predicate must prove entitlement and tenant/job scope before returning data. Test direct API access as well as rendered UI; hiding a link is not authorization.
11. Client sign-in tokens are audience-, job-, and action-scoped; short-lived, single-use, revocable, and excluded from URLs/logs after redemption. A valid client session is not a staff actor.
12. The public demo contains curated synthetic data. Synthetic CI fixtures are eligible for promotion only after provenance, sanitization, privacy review, and explicit allowlisting; customer-like data, CFS-derived payloads, private domains, secrets, and real provider messages are excluded.
13. Upgrade and uninstall semantics preserve customer-owned records and attachments. Deleting app metadata is not permission to delete customer data; cleanup is explicit, previewed, and separately authorized.
14. A public release, marketplace publication, real customer email, production install, or destructive migration needs an explicit owner approval at the point of action. Planning this work is not that approval.

name: twenty-develop-app
description: Use when developing or modifying a Twenty app.
---

# When To Use

Pick this skill when the user wants to change what an existing Twenty app *does* — its data model, UI, logic, or workflows. Representative triggers:

- "add a new object to my Twenty app"
- "create a logic function that runs on record create"
- "add a custom field to the company object"
- "build a front component for the deal page"
- "modify an existing entity / object / field"
- "add a workflow with a manual trigger"
- "add roles and permissions to my app"
- "create a standalone page in my app"

Do not use this skill to scaffold a brand-new app (use `create-app`), to sync/deploy/troubleshoot (use `manage-app`), to prepare marketplace assets (use `publish-app`), or to query workspace records (use `use-twenty-mcp`).

# Boundaries

For background on how Twenty apps work — the SDK packages, remotes, sync lifecycle, and rendering model — read `../twenty-official-references/references/concepts/how-apps-work.md`.

Do not scaffold a new app here. Use `create-app` first when the app does not exist.

# Workflow

First, confirm the setup is sane before changing entities. The current directory should be the root of an existing Twenty app:

```bash
test -f package.json
test -f src/application-config.ts
```

If either file is missing, do not edit blindly. Inspect nearby folders to find the app root, or use `create-app` when the app does not exist.

If setup, dependencies, remotes, authentication, sync, build, deploy, logs, or CI/CD are failing, switch to `manage-app` before continuing with entity work.

For app shape and entity file structure, read `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/app-structure.md`.

## Plan Before Editing

For any change involving more than one entity, state the plan back in 3–6 lines before editing: objects extended, fields added, logic functions and post-install hooks declared, whether the app needs UI. Confirm with the user when there is a real choice.

Skip for single-entity edits, renames, and copy fixes.

## Code Organization

Keep logic functions, post-install hooks, and front components narrow. Extract everything that is not the trigger, inputs, writes, rendering shell, or external call:

- `src/utils/<name>.util.ts` — pure helpers (parsers, mappers, formatters).
- `src/front-components/utils/<name>.util.ts` — front-component runtime helpers that are reusable and testable.
- `src/types/<name>.ts` — external API and internal DTO types (one PascalCase type per file).
- `src/<service>-client/<name>.ts` — wrappers around external SDKs or shared HTTP clients. One folder per service, matching Twenty's `*-client` convention.

Kebab-case filenames. One export per file is mandatory for every helper, type, and client file in `src/` — never multiple function exports in one file. The rule counts exports: a local (non-exported) type may stay alongside the util, but once a type is exported or reused it splits into a `src/types/<name>.ts` file separate from the `src/utils/<name>.util.ts` file. See `app-structure.md` for the canonical rule and the full suffix convention.

Refactor when:

- A `*.logic-function.ts` or `*.post-install.ts` file exceeds the soft cap (see `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/logic.md`).
- A front component contains duplicated command execution, record loading, logic-function lookup, payload building, result parsing, or snackbar formatting.
- The same parsing or mapping logic appears across object types.
- Multiple field files differ only by name and identifier — use a factory under `src/fields/`.

Always create a `*.spec.ts` test file in a sibling `__tests__/` folder for every util/function you add or change, one spec file per source file. See `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/tests.md`.

When a front component triggers a logic function for selected records, always prefer a bulk-capable logic function unless the user explicitly states that the function is only for one record. The default payload shape is `records: Array<{ id: string; ...fields }>`: inside `records`, use `id` for the Twenty record ID because the array name already establishes the record context. Do not add flat single-record compatibility payloads unless the user explicitly asks to preserve an existing single-record API.

## Adding New Entities

Use the app CLI to add new entities. It generates the correct file structure, UUIDs, SDK imports, and boilerplate automatically:

```bash
yarn twenty dev:add
```

This is the default and preferred way to create objects, fields, views, logic functions, front components, and other entities. Do not manually create entity files, explore SDK typings in `node_modules`, or generate UUIDs by hand when the CLI can do it.

Only create entity files manually when modifying existing entities or when the CLI does not support the specific entity type.

## After Entity Changes

Once all edits for the change are complete, run lint and typecheck once at the end (not after each individual edit), then sync the app to the active remote:

```bash
yarn twenty dev:typecheck
yarn lint
yarn twenty apply
```

`yarn twenty dev:typecheck` checks generated app types, `yarn lint` checks local lint rules, and `yarn twenty apply` syncs entity definitions to the active remote. Run all three a single time once every edit is done, not repeatedly after each step. When the user explicitly asks to run tests, follow `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/tests.md`.

Use the official Twenty docs or local SDK source when exact entity fields, imports, or configuration shapes matter.

# Develop References

Read the smallest reference that matches the requested entity work:

- Objects, fields, relations, roles, and permissions: `../twenty-official-references/references/develop-app/data-model.md`

# beads-bv — Graph-Aware Triage

<!-- TOC: Robot Mode | Commands | Workflow | Scoping | Metrics | br | Troubleshooting | References -->

> **Core Insight:** Your backlog is a directed graph. PageRank finds what everything depends on. Betweenness finds bottlenecks. The math knows your priorities better than your gut.

## CRITICAL: Robot Mode Only

```bash
bv                    # WRONG — launches TUI, blocks terminal
bv --robot-triage     # CORRECT — JSON output for agents
```

**NEVER run bare `bv` in agent contexts.**

---

## Commands

### Core (Start Here)

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-triage` | THE MEGA-COMMAND: recommendations + blockers + health | What should I work on? |
| `--robot-next` | Single top pick + claim command | Just the one thing |
| `--robot-plan` | Parallel execution tracks with `unblocks` | What can run concurrently? |
| `--robot-insights` | All metrics + cycles + density + k-core + slack | Deep analysis |
| `--robot-priority` | Priority misalignments with confidence | Am I prioritizing wrong? |

### Labels & Health

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-label-health` | Per-label: health_level, velocity, staleness | Which domain is struggling? |
| `--robot-label-flow` | Cross-label dependencies, bottleneck_labels | Inter-team blockers |
| `--robot-label-attention` | Attention-ranked labels | Where to focus? |
| `--robot-alerts` | Stale issues, blocking cascades, priority mismatches | What's rotting? |
| `--robot-suggest` | Duplicates, missing deps, cycle breaks | Hygiene |

### History & Correlation

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-history` | Bead-to-commit correlations | Change tracking |
| `--robot-causality <id>` | Timeline, blockers, insights | Why did this take so long? |
| `--robot-related <id>` | File/commit overlap, clusters | What's connected? |
| `--robot-file-beads <path>` | Beads that touched a file | Code ownership |

### Time-Travel & Search

| Command | Returns | Use When |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `--robot-diff --diff-since <ref>` | New/closed/modified since ref | What changed? |
| `--as-of <ref>` | Historical point-in-time | Time-travel |
| `--robot-search` | Search results as JSON | Find beads |
| `--search-mode hybrid` | Text + graph ranking | Smart search |

**Full command reference:** [COMMANDS.md](references/COMMANDS.md)

---

## Workflow

```bash
# 1. What should I work on?
bv --robot-triage | jq '.triage.recommendations[0]'

# 2. Claim it
br update bd-123 --status in_progress

# 3. Do the work...

# 4. Done
br close bd-123 --reason "Implemented in abc123"

# 5. Next
bv --robot-triage
```

---

## Scoping & Filtering

```bash
bv --robot-plan --label backend              # Scope to label's subgraph
bv --robot-insights --as-of HEAD~30          # Historical point-in-time
bv --recipe actionable --robot-plan          # Only unblocked items
bv --recipe high-impact --robot-triage       # Top PageRank scores
bv --robot-triage --robot-triage-by-track    # Group by parallel streams
bv --robot-triage --robot-triage-by-label    # Group by domain
bv --robot-alerts --severity=critical        # Filter alerts
```

---

## Key Metrics

| Metric | High Score Means |
|--------|------------------|
| **PageRank** | Everything depends on this — fix first |
| **Betweenness** | Bottleneck — blocks multiple paths |
| **Cycles** | **Broken graph — fix immediately** |
| **K-Core** | Structural strength (core membership) |
| **Articulation** | Cut vertex — removal disconnects graph |

### Decision Matrix

| Pattern | Meaning | Action |
|---------|---------|--------|
| High PageRank + High Betweenness | Critical bottleneck | Drop everything, fix this |
| High PageRank + Low Betweenness | Foundation piece | Important but not blocking |
| Low PageRank + High Betweenness | Unexpected chokepoint | Investigate why |

**Full metrics:** [METRICS.md](references/METRICS.md)

---

## br Essentials

```bash
br ready --json                              # What's unblocked?
br create "Title" -d "desc"                  # New issue
br update bd-123 --status in_progress        # Working on this
br close bd-123 --reason "Done"              # Done
br dep add bd-123 bd-456                      # Add dependency
br dep remove bd-123 bd-456                   # Break cycle
```

---

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `bv` hangs | TUI launched | Use `--robot-*` flags |
| Cycles detected | Circular dependency | `br dep remove` to break |
| Phase 2 timeout | Large graph (>500 nodes) | Check `status` field |
| Empty metric maps | Phase 2 still running | Check `status` flags |
| Inconsistent outputs | Different data | Compare `data_hash` |

---

## Validation

```bash
# Tools working?
bv --robot-triage >/dev/null && br list >/dev/null && echo "OK"

# Graph healthy?
bv --robot-insights | jq '{cycles: .Cycles, density: .ClusterDensity}'
# cycles must be [], density < 0.3 is healthy
```

---

| All metrics explained | [METRICS.md](references/METRICS.md) |
| jq recipes, morning triage | [RECIPES.md](references/RECIPES.md) |

# Planning Prompts — Complete Reference

## Table of Contents
- [Plan Review (GPT Pro)](#plan-review-gpt-pro)
- [Integrate Revisions (Claude Code)](#integrate-revisions-claude-code)
- [Multi-Model Blend (GPT Pro)](#multi-model-blend-gpt-pro)
- [Initial Plan Creation](#initial-plan-creation)

---

## Plan Review (GPT Pro)

Use with GPT Pro with Extended Reasoning enabled. Paste your entire markdown plan:

```
Carefully review this entire plan for me and come up with your best revisions in terms of better architecture, new features, changed features, etc. to make it better, more robust/reliable, more performant, more compelling/useful, etc. For each proposed change, give me your detailed analysis and rationale/justification for why it would make the project better along with the git-diff style change versus the original plan shown below:

<PASTE YOUR EXISTING COMPLETE PLAN HERE>
```

---

## Integrate Revisions (Claude Code)

After GPT Pro finishes (may take 20-30 minutes for complex plans), paste the output into Claude Code:

```
OK, now integrate these revisions to the markdown plan in-place; use ultrathink and be meticulous. At the end, you can tell me which changes you wholeheartedly agree with, which you somewhat agree with, and which you disagree with:

```[Pasted text from GPT Pro]```
```

### Repeat Until Steady-State

- Start fresh ChatGPT conversations for each round
- After 4-5 rounds, suggestions become very incremental
- You'll see massive improvements from v2 to v3, continuing to the end
- This phase can take 2-3 hours for complex features — this is normal

---

## Multi-Model Blend (GPT Pro)

Get competing plans from Gemini 3.1 Pro (Deep Think), Grok4 Heavy, and Opus 4.7, then use GPT Pro as final arbiter:

```
I asked 3 competing LLMs to do the exact same thing and they came up with pretty different plans which you can read below. I want you to REALLY carefully analyze their plans with an open mind and be intellectually honest about what they did that's better than your plan. Then I want you to come up with the best possible revisions to your plan (you should simply update your existing document for your original plan with the revisions) that artfully and skillfully blends the "best of all worlds" to create a true, ultimate, superior hybrid version of the plan that best achieves our stated goals and will work the best in real-world practice to solve the problems we are facing and our overarching goals while ensuring the extreme success of the enterprise as best as possible; you should provide me with a complete series of git-diff style changes to your original plan to turn it into the new, enhanced, much longer and detailed plan that integrates the best of all the plans with every good idea included (you don't need to mention which ideas came from which models in the final revised enhanced plan):

[Paste competing plans here]
```

---

## Initial Plan Creation

When starting a new project, include:

1. **Goals and Intent** — What you're really trying to accomplish
2. **Workflows** — How the final software should work from the user's perspective
3. **Tech Stack** — Be specific (e.g., "TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind, Supabase")
4. **Architecture Decisions** — High-level structure and patterns
5. **The "Why"** — The more the model understands your end goal, the better it performs

You don't even need to write the initial markdown plan yourself. You can write that with GPT Pro, just explaining what it is you want to make.

3:**Pane 2 — GPT-6 Luna, 2026-09-29**  
4:**Scope:** read-only inspection of localbench `create`, `keep`, `pull`, `show`, and `why`, plus pinned Ollama v0.34.4 create/Modelfile semantics. No code, Beads, reports/packets, profiles, model actions, inference, or private reads changed or performed.
5:
6:## Decision
7:
8:**Reject a model-recipe feature for now. Do not create a Bead.** The current recorded operator problem is slow local OMP; the packet attributes the suspected cold delay to OMP sending about 74,289 prompt tokens, not to a missing Modelfile operation. No user has named a recipe setting, task failure, or reliability problem that this missing operation would fix. A recipe can alter prompt formatting/system content and runtime parameters, but there is no evidence that a particular change reduces this OMP request without failing MUST behavior. A known-good/known-bad/no-op recipe trio would therefore be invented rather than a real, nonduplicate trial.
9:
10:`localbench create` is narrower than Ollama’s recipe interface, but “Ollama can create a model” is not itself a localbench product need. Localbench adds controlled operator behavior around its supported create path; extending that path is justified only by a named OMP use case whose value cannot be obtained with current OMP flags or an already-supported artifact.
11:
12:## Observed operator behavior
13:
14:| Command | What the operator can actually do | What it does not establish for a recipe |
15:|---|---|---|
16:| `localbench create ollama:<name> --from <safetensors-dir>` | Builds from a local Safetensors directory; optional quantization; `--like` copies an existing model’s OMP renderer/parser, or either can be overridden. `--dry-run`/`--explain` plan the action. It refuses while a run is alive and refuses an existing name rather than replacing it. It writes a generated `Modelfile.localbench` containing `FROM <dir>` and selected `RENDERER`/`PARSER`, invokes `ollama create` with the configured model store, then reads back model details and prints the installed digest. | No arbitrary user Modelfile, no `FROM` an installed model name, and no user-selected `TEMPLATE`, `SYSTEM`, `PARAMETER`, `MESSAGE`, or `REQUIRES` inputs. The printed digest is not visibly copied into `…
17:| `localbench keep ollama:<model> [duration]` | Sets a finite residency lease (default 5m); verifies resident state after the request. A zero/unload request refuses during a live run, when resident state is unknown, or unless external/gateway activity is proved safe; “not loaded” is a no-op. Lease expiry is surfaced to localbench status. | Residency control, not model construction, recipe storage, or recipe comparison. |
18:| `localbench pull ollama:<model>` | Pulls/updates a registry tag through Ollama `/api/pull`, streams progress, then confirms the installed tag and digest. Refuses while a localbench run is alive. Its separate `hf:<org>/<repo>` path downloads files at the API-reported revision, records source metadata, checks disk headroom, and can resume. | Installs source artifacts; it does not build a derived recipe. The ordinary Ollama-tag path confirms the digest in CLI output, but the inspected handler does not place that digest in `Mutation.detail`. |
19:| `localbench show <receipt|golden|run-dir>` | Renders receipts, goldens, or run summaries; `--path` selects an unrounded JSON subtree; `--diff` compares a golden with a git revision. | Not `ollama show`; it does not inspect an arbitrary installed model or display its Modelfile. During `create`, the handler separately calls Ollama `/api/show` for renderer/parser/capabilities. |
20:| `localbench why <audit-id>` | Reads one mutation-ledger row: verb, outcome, time, original argv, cwd, host, localbench version, actions, and recorded details. `Mutation` records done/refused/failed outcomes; a dry run writes no ledger row. | It explains the localbench invocation and recorded detail; it does not itself query Ollama or prove a model recipe’s quality, OMP compatibility, or performance. |
21:
22:These differences are useful safeguards and observability in the existing localbench-owned workflows. They are not evidence that users need arbitrary recipe authoring.
23:
24:## Pinned upstream contract and the duplication boundary
25:
26:Ollama v0.34.4 documents `POST /api/create` as creating from an existing model, a Safetensors directory, or GGUF files. Its request can include `from`, file digests, `template`, `renderer`, `parser`, `license`, `system`, `parameters`, `messages`, and `quantize`; progress is streamed. The same tag’s Modelfile reference describes `FROM`, `PARAMETER`, `TEMPLATE`, `SYSTEM`, `LICENSE`, `MESSAGE`, and `REQUIRES`. `PARAMETER` includes `num_ctx`, sampling settings, stop sequences, and token limits.
27:
28:Thus arbitrary recipe construction is already an Ollama capability. A localbench wrapper could be operationally distinct by applying the repository’s required CLI policy, dry-run/explain, run-state/name-collision protection, correct server model-store targeting, and audit/readback. But the proposed user-facing action still duplicates Ollama’s recipe semantics. A wrapper only has a product wedge if a real OMP task requires that controlled path and its existing create subset cannot serve it.
29:
30:### Current mission does not supply that need
31:
32:The packet identifies one user and one machine; the current success condition is a MUST-conformant OMP tool turn at or below 10 seconds, compared against the pinned incumbent in the same invocation. Its current slow-path hypothesis is a very large OMP prompt (about 74k tokens) and cold prefill. The packet also rules out remote/cloud fallback and model-weight patching. Nothing inspected identifies an OMP failure attributable to the model’s Modelfile, nor a `TEMPLATE`, `SYSTEM`, or `PARAMETER` edit that would remove the measured delay while preserving tool-call and thinking behavior. Changing `num_ctx` could constrain/truncate usable context; changing a template or system message could alter semantics. Neither effect is a proven solution here.
33:
34:## Trial choice and limits
35:
36:**No known-good / known-bad / no-op recipe choice is authorized or evidence-based today.** No real need specifies which source, recipe directive, OMP task, or observable benefit to test. Selecting a parameter value merely to populate a control set would invent the requirement. Correct no-op: do not create a derivative, do not edit a profile, and do not add a Bead.
37:

# mcp__mcp_agent_mail_list_agents — mcp-agent-mail/list_agents

List registered agents in a project, most-recently-active first.

Returns agent name, role (program), model, task description, registration time (inception_ts), and last seen (last_active_ts).

The result is bounded to avoid blowing the calling agent's context window on long-lived projects that accumulate agents across many short-lived swarms: at most `limit` agents (default 250) are returned, optionally restricted to those active within `active_within_days`.

Parameters
----------
project_key : str
    Project slug or human key.
limit : Optional[int]
    Maximum number of agents to return (most-recently-active first). Defaults to 250; values above 250 are clamped to 250.
active_within_days : Optional[int]
    If provided, only return agents whose last_active_ts is within this many days. Omit to include all agents (subject to limit).

Returns
-------
str (JSON)
    Array of agent objects with fields: name, program, model, task_description, inception_ts, last_active_ts, contact_policy. Ordered by last_active_ts descending.

## Schema
```ts
type Args = {
  project_key: string;

};
